text:
BBVFD flood relief drive aids West Virginia storm victims as recovery efforts continue
BRUCETON MILLS, W.Va. — Over the weekend, officials with the Bruceton Brandonville Volunteer Fire Department delivered two trucks and trailers packed with flood relief items to Lewis and Upshur counties, thanks to overwhelming support from the local community.
Last week through noon on Saturday, BBVFD officials collected donations at the station to aid ongoing relief efforts for communities hit by severe flooding in Upshur, Lewis, and Pleasants counties.
Department officials expressed their gratitude to everyone who donated and supported the effort. They noted that the BBVFD is still accepting monetary donations, which will be directed to the areas of greatest need.
Due to the severity of the flooding, officials said recovery and cleanup efforts will likely take months.
The relief drive followed the department’s initial emergency response, during which members of the BBVFD Swiftwater rescue team deployed to assist impacted areas.
Department Chief John Vincent said that during the initial response, crews performed 75 rescues in the city of Weston alone.
“It was the worst flooding I’ve seen in 30 years of fire service,” he added.
Melissa Kent, vice president of the BBVFD, said the local community consistently steps up during times of need.
Recalling previous relief drives, Kent noted that a past collection for Grant County ran for five days and filled an entire trailer.
Compared to past drives, the community’s response to this effort was even faster.
Kent said the department posted about the drive on Wednesday and accepted donations only through Saturday morning. Despite the short timeframe, the trailer was three-quarters full with essential, high-value goods.
“Several people donated shovels, rakes and other high-ticket items,” she said. “It doesn’t surprise me with our community because that’s what they do.”
The department has hosted numerous fundraisers over the years, and community members always gather to support those efforts, she added.
Kent explained that the short donation window was intentional because flood victims need immediate access to cleaning supplies to begin reclaiming their homes.
“That was the goal,” she said. “They need to have things immediately.”
Although the recent flooding did not directly hit Preston County, the destruction reminded many residents of the region’s historic 1985 flood.
However, officials noted that major rivers were not the primary cause of this disaster. Instead, small creeks and waterways overflowed rapidly, demonstrating how fast and heavy the rain fell during the storm.
Kent added that one of the most devastating aspects of the storm was that many affected homes were not located in designated flood zones, leaving residents without flood insurance.
Assistant Chief Ian Kent and his wife, Amber, assisted with a mobile shower and laundry station in Weston.
While there, they spoke with multiple victims who explained they lacked flood insurance because they believed they did not need it. Because the destruction was caused by rising water, standard homeowners insurance policies will not cover the damage.
“Some people have lost everything,” Melissa Kent said.
Officials noted that many residents who lost nearly everything have little to no financial recourse to rebuild, forcing them to start over entirely.
However, Kent emphasized that West Virginians always pull together in times of crisis.
“That is one thing about our state overall, we stick tight and help each other through the good times and the bad,” she said.
While the BBVFD’s initial supply drive has concluded, other relief programs remain active throughout the county.
Department officials advised anyone interested in helping to contact local donation centers in the affected counties. A full list of collection sites is available on the official City of Weston Facebook page.
